Section: Modules and Packages / Module System

# Modules

A module is a `.kedi` source file compiled as part of a root program. Its
top-level code initializes module state; its export directive selects which
bindings are published to importers.

## Module Files and Paths

Given:

```text
project/
  main.kedi
  services/
    users.kedi
    audit.kedi
```

`main.kedi` imports the nested files without suffixes:

```kedi
> import: services/users
> import: services/audit

= <user_count()> users
```

Each slash-separated segment must be a valid identifier. Absolute paths,
`.`/`..`, backslashes, empty segments, and a written `.kedi` suffix are not
module names.

## Relative Resolution

The first candidate is relative to the file containing the import, not the
process working directory and not always the root program:

```text
project/
  main.kedi
  features/
    report.kedi
    formatting.kedi
```

An import of `formatting` inside `features/report.kedi` resolves to
`features/formatting.kedi`. Use this property to keep feature-local module
graphs relocatable.

A source compiled only from an in-memory string has no relative directory.
Without a source path it can import registered bundled modules, but unresolved
file modules produce an error explaining that a source path is required.

## Resolution Order

For each import Kedi checks:

1. the importer-relative `.kedi` path;
2. a bundled internal module with that name;
3. the installed package registry.

The first existing file wins. Registry validation is deferred until local and
built-in candidates miss, so a corrupt installed package cannot break a valid
higher-priority local import.

## Package Modules

For an installed package `kedi_http`:

```kedi
> import: kedi_http
> import: kedi_http/client
```

The root import resolves the package source's `main.kedi`; the second resolves
`client.kedi`. Installed paths are checked for containment, symlink escapes,
manifest validity, package-name agreement, and source layout before loading.

## Initialization Once per Compilation

A resolved module executes at most once for one root compilation. Later imports
reuse its initialized exports and publish those bindings at each import
statement's source position.

This prevents duplicate prelude and top-level side effects in a diamond:

```text
main -> reports -> shared
     -> alerts  -> shared
```

`shared.kedi` initializes once, even though both branches import it. A separate
root compilation initializes it again; module state is not a process-global
singleton.

## Module Prelude and Side Effects

A module may begin with a Python prelude and may execute top-level statements:

````kedi
```
import re
PATTERN = re.compile(r"^[a-z0-9-]+$")
```

@valid_slug(value: str) -> bool:
  = `PATTERN.fullmatch(value) is not None`

> export:
  valid_slug
````

Prelude failures fail module initialization and therefore the importing
program. Keep initialization lightweight and deterministic. Network calls,
filesystem writes, and mutable global setup are usually better placed in
explicit procedures.

## Cycles and Missing Modules

Do not design cyclic module imports. A module graph should flow from higher-level
features toward lower-level shared modules. Missing modules report the searched
candidate paths; invalid module segments fail before filesystem lookup.

Use the LSP's definition and diagnostics support to inspect resolution rather
than compensating with working-directory-dependent paths.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/imports-and-exports.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Module System

# Imports and Exports

Imports publish selected module bindings directly into the current source
environment. Exports are explicit so implementation helpers remain private.

## Import a Module

```kedi
> import: profiles

= `get_profile("Ada")`
```

The imported module must explicitly export `get_profile`. Imports do not bind a
`profiles` namespace and do not expose unexported names. The backtick expression
preserves the native `Profile`. An angle call such as `<get_profile(Ada)>`
renders text, and a `Profile` has no text form, so it is a type error there.
An ordinary `<name>` value substitution renders to text too.

## Explicit Exports

In `profiles.kedi`:

```kedi
~Profile(name: str, id: int)

@get_profile(name: str) -> Profile:
  = `Profile(name=name, id=1)`

@normalize_internal(name: str) -> str:
  = `name.strip()`

[profile_id: int] = `1`

> export:
  Profile
  get_profile
  profile_id
```

`normalize_internal` remains usable inside the module but is unavailable to
importers. An export name must resolve to a top-level declaration or value in
that module.

## Selective Imports

An importer can request only part of the exported surface:

```kedi
> import: services/profiles:
  Profile
  get_profile
```

Every selected name must be exported by the target and must appear once in the
list. A missing, private, or duplicate name is an error. Selective import is
appropriate for documenting dependencies and avoiding collisions in large
programs.

## Star Exports

`> export: *` exports every public top-level name except the runtime-owned `args`
binding. Imported procedures still read the caller's CLI arguments; those
arguments are not re-exported or rebound by the import. Explicitly importing
an exported `args` binding is rejected because the name is reserved.

```kedi
@public_name() -> str:
  = visible

@_internal_name() -> str:
  = hidden

> export: *
```

Names beginning with `_` remain private. Star export is convenient for small
facade modules, but explicit export lists make API reviews and compatibility
changes clearer.

## Re-Exports

Because imported names enter the module environment, an importing module can
export them again:

```kedi
> import: services/profiles:
  Profile

@load_default() -> Profile:
  = `Profile(name="default", id=0)`

> export:
  Profile
  load_default
```

Use re-exports to create a stable facade. Avoid chains of accidental star
re-exports, which make ownership and compatibility difficult to see.

## Source-Order Binding

Imports and declarations bind names where they appear. When several statements
provide the same name, the last binding wins:

```kedi
[label] = before
> import: labels
[label] = after

= <label>
```

The result is `"after"`. This behavior supports deliberate overrides but can
hide collisions. Prefer selective imports or distinct names when both values
matter.

An initialized module's exports are republished at every import position, so a
later repeated import can overwrite a binding changed between imports without
re-running module initialization.

## Private and Non-Exported Names

No export directive means the module publishes nothing. A leading underscore
only matters to star export; an explicit export list should still be used for
the intended public API.

Module Python-prelude helpers are implementation details unless surfaced through
a Kedi value, procedure, type, or profile and explicitly exported.

## Errors

Kedi rejects invalid paths, missing module files, unknown selective names,
duplicate names in one selective list, unknown exports, and malformed export
directives. Import errors include the resolution candidates so local,
built-in, and registry problems can be distinguished.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/built-in-modules.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Standard Modules

# Built-In Modules

Kedi ships a small set of ordinary `.kedi` modules. They use the same explicit
exports, profiles, Python interop, tool metadata, and resolution rules as project
modules.


## Resolution and Shadowing

Import a bundled module by name:

```kedi
> import: filesystem:
  readonlyfs
  read_text_file
```

A sibling `filesystem.kedi` takes precedence over the bundled module. Use this
deliberately; an accidental same-name file changes the imported API.


## `errors`

The `errors` module exports `ModuleNotInstalledError`:

````kedi
> import: errors

```
raise ModuleNotInstalledError("httpx", required_by="HTTP reports")
```
````

The exception subclasses `ModuleNotFoundError` and formats singular or plural
missing package names. Use it when a feature has a clear optional Python
dependency.


## `require`

`require` exports a Python-callable helper:

````kedi
> import: require

```
require(["httpx", "pydantic"], required_by="Remote reports")
```
````

It checks import availability with Python's module discovery and returns `True`
when all names are present. Missing modules raise `ModuleNotInstalledError`.
It does not install packages or validate their versions.


## `filesystem`

`filesystem` exports `filesystem`, `readonlyfs`, `read_text_file`,
`write_text_file`, `apply_patch`, `path_exists`, `list_directory`,
`create_directory`, `remove_file`, `remove_directory`, and `get_file_info`.
See [`filesystem`](filesystem.md) for the full table.

## `media`

`media` exports the loaders `image`, `audio`, `video` and `document`, `save`,
which writes a media value to a file, and the types `Media`, `Image`, `Audio`,
`Video` and `Document`. See
[Multimodal Input](../core-language/multimodal-input.md).

## `sandbox`

The optional `sandbox` module exports `execute_code` and a `sandbox` profile:

```kedi
> import: sandbox

[result: Any] = `execute_code("sum(values)", {"values": [1, 2, 3]})`
```

It requires the Python package `pydantic_monty`. Importing the module checks that
dependency immediately. `execute_code(code, inputs={}, fail_fast=False)` executes
with Monty and returns the native final result; the backtick expression preserves
that value. Inputs default to an empty mapping. Execution failures are returned as
text by default so an agent can inspect them; pass `fail_fast=True` to raise instead.

This sandbox is for intentionally constrained generated code. It is not the
execution mechanism for ordinary Kedi Python blocks, which use the configured
Kedi executor.

## `helpers`

`helpers` exports `llm_approval(request: ApprovalRequest) -> ApprovalDecision`,
an experimental model-backed approval handler. It requires tool reasons to be
enabled on the calling tool surface; the model's reason is untrusted context,
not proof of user authorization. The helper produces and displays assessed
risk, authorization confidence, an allow/deny decision, and a concise
rationale. A denial returns the same report to the calling model through the
adapter's denied tool result. It does not run for ordinary read-only calls.

```kedi
> import: helpers:
  llm_approval

> settings:
  tool_reason: enabled
> approval: `llm_approval`
```

This configures the handler; it does not invoke a tool by itself. Select a
compatible model and explicit tool scope before using it. Keep deterministic
allowlists or human review for decisions that require stronger guarantees.
See [Tool Reasons](../agentic-engineering/tool-reasons.md).


## `this` and Example Modules

`this` is a bundled demonstration/easter-egg module whose import executes its
encoded output. It is not an application API.

`wordle` exports its game profile and game procedures; it requires a graphical
environment and optional packages. Its exports are `WordleSetup`,
`GuessValidation`, the `wordle` profile, `prepare_wordle_setup`,
`validate_wordle_guess`, `play_wordle`, and `play_default_wordle`. See
[Example Modules](example-modules.md) for the export table. These are
demonstrations, not general-purpose stdlib contracts.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/filesystem.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Standard Modules

# Filesystem Module

Import the tools you need or apply a profile. Workspace containment, secret-file opt-in, risk classification, and approval are separate checks; ordinary Python execution is not sandboxed by this module.

## `filesystem`

The `filesystem` module exports:

| Name | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `read_text_file` | Read one UTF-8 file |
| `write_text_file` | Replace/create one UTF-8 file |
| `apply_patch` | Add, append, or exact-once replace text |
| `path_exists` | Check file or directory existence |
| `list_directory` | Return sorted direct child names |
| `create_directory` | Create a directory tree |
| `remove_file` | Delete one file |
| `remove_directory` | Delete a directory tree |
| `get_file_info` | Return basic path metadata |
| `filesystem` | Read/write agent profile |
| `readonlyfs` | Read-only agent profile |

```kedi
> import: filesystem

@load_readme() -> str:
  = `read_text_file("README.md")`
```

## Workspace Policy

Paths resolve against the process working directory captured when the module
initializes, not a later working-directory change. `KEDI_WORKSPACE_POLICY`
selects containment at access time:

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Unset, empty, or `strict` | Resolved path must remain under the captured root, including after symlink resolution |
| `none` | Disable workspace containment; absolute and outside-root paths are permitted subject to other checks and OS permissions |
| Any other value | Configuration error rather than fallback |

`none` does not disable secret-file checks, delete protection, tool approval, or
read/list bounds. Avoid selecting it for untrusted agent workloads merely to
make a failing path work. Ordinary embedded Python can bypass these helpers;
host isolation is still necessary for untrusted programs.

## Bounded Reads

`read_text_file(file_path, secret_files=False, offset=0, max_chars=-1)` returns
UTF-8 text. `offset` is a nonnegative character offset, not a byte offset.
`max_chars=-1` permits an unbounded read only for files up to 1,000,000 bytes.
For larger files, pass a positive character limit. Zero and values below -1
are invalid. Direct calls return `str`; agent calls stream internally into
artifact admission without changing the declared return schema.

```kedi
> import: filesystem:
  read_text_file

# Requires an existing application.log in the workspace.
[head] = `read_text_file("application.log", max_chars=2000)`
[next_page] = `read_text_file("application.log", offset=2000, max_chars=2000)`
= <head>\n<next_page>
```

This is two bounded pages, not a claim that the file ends there. Directory
listing remains capped at 1,000 direct entries and returns alphabetically
sorted names; it has no pagination parameter.

## Secrets and Approval

Files named `.env` or beginning `.env.` are treated as secrets.
`read_text_file(path)` refuses them unless `secret_files=True`. In agent tool
use, that argument changes the call's risk classification so approval can be
required. Secret opt-in is not an authorization boundary by itself; the host
approval policy still decides.

## Exact Patches

`apply_patch("add", ...)` refuses an existing file. `update` requires a nonempty
`old_text` that occurs exactly once. `append` adds content. Prefer `apply_patch`
over whole-file writes for auditable agent edits.

When invoked as an agent tool, expected edit conflicts (an existing add target,
empty/missing/ambiguous `old_text`, or an invalid operation) return an explicit
`Patch rejected; no changes made` result. The agent can inspect the current file
and correct its edit without exhausting framework validation retries. Direct
programmatic calls still raise for these conflicts. Permission, path-boundary,
and unexpected I/O errors still propagate; replacement remains exact-once, never
fuzzy.

## Profiles and Destructive Operations

`readonlyfs` registers reads and metadata only. `filesystem` additionally
registers writes, patching, directory creation, and the destructive
`remove_file` and `remove_directory` tools. Removal cannot target the filesystem
captured workspace root, filesystem anchor, or user's home directory, including
under `KEDI_WORKSPACE_POLICY=none`. Agent approval still applies to destructive
calls. Direct Python/Kedi procedure calls retain path checks but are not an
agent tool approval loop.

## Callable Contracts

| Callable | Arguments and native result |
| --- | --- |
| `write_text_file` | `file_path, content` -> resolved path string; creates parents |
| `apply_patch` | `operation, file_path, content="", old_text="", new_text=""` -> edit summary; add/update/append only |
| `path_exists` | `path` -> bool |
| `list_directory` | `dir_path` -> sorted `list[str]` |
| `create_directory` | `dir_path` -> resolved path string; creates parents |
| `remove_file` | `file_path` -> deleted path string; missing target raises |
| `remove_directory` | `dir_path` -> deleted path string; recursively removes contents |
| `get_file_info` | `path` -> dict with `path`, `name`, `is_file`, `is_dir`, `size` (bytes), `modified_time` (timestamp) |

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/example-modules.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Standard Modules

# Example Modules

These modules demonstrate Kedi composition. Importing them can execute Python
setup; they are not guaranteed to work in a headless or dependency-free host.

## Wordle

`wordle` exports:

| Export | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `WordleSetup` | Typed generated game setup |
| `GuessValidation` | Typed guess assessment |
| `wordle` | Game agent profile |
| `prepare_wordle_setup(theme, seed_hint, blocked_answers)` | Model-backed setup procedure |
| `validate_wordle_guess(guess)` | Model-backed guess validator |
| `play_wordle(theme)` | Graphical game session, returns its summary |
| `play_default_wordle()` | Starts the default everyday-objects theme |

The graphical path needs its optional dependencies and a display. Model-backed
procedures also need a configured provider. Import only the explicit exports
you intend to call; private rendering and scoring helpers are implementation
details. Do not use this game module as a general schema for production agents.

## This

`this` prints its bundled demonstration text during module initialization. It
does not define a reusable application API. A separate root compilation may
execute that import-time effect again, consistent with ordinary module lifetime.

# Package Manifests

`package.kedi` is a declarative package manifest written in Kedi directive
syntax. It is not an executable module.

## Complete Manifest

```kedi
> package: kedi_http:
  version: 1.2.0
  source: src/kedi_http
  python: python@3.11-3.14
  python_dependencies:
    httpx>=0.27
    pydantic>=2
```

The file must be named exactly `package.kedi` and contain exactly one package
directive. Comments are allowed; imports, exports, procedures, custom types,
Python blocks, variable initializations, assignments, and other executable
statements are rejected.

## Package Name

Package names use lowercase ASCII letters, digits, and underscores, start with a
letter, and match the installed registry directory:

```text
kedi_http    valid
http2        valid
KediHTTP     invalid
kedi-http    invalid
2http        invalid
```

The package name is also the root module name used by importers.

## Version

`version` is optional but, when present, must be a valid PEP 440 version:

```kedi
> package: reports:
  version: 2.0.0rc1
  source: src/reports
```

The manifest version is package metadata. It does not select a Python
environment or automatically enforce API compatibility between packages.

## Source Directory and `main.kedi`

`source` is required for installation. It is a literal relative directory
inside the package root and must contain `main.kedi`:

```text
package.kedi
src/
  kedi_http/
    main.kedi
    client.kedi
```

For `source: src/kedi_http`, `> import: kedi_http` loads `main.kedi` and
`> import: kedi_http/client` loads `client.kedi`.

Absolute paths, parent traversal, symlink escapes, sparse-checkout metacharacters
such as `*`, missing directories, and a source without `main.kedi` are rejected.

## Python Version Requirement

The optional `python` field accepts only:

```text
python@3.11
python@3.11-3.14
```

The range is closed and inclusive. The upper version cannot precede the lower
version. Installation checks the interpreter running the installer and refuses
an incompatible package.

This field expresses host compatibility, not a dependency to install.

## Python Dependencies

`python_dependencies` is an indented list of PEP 508 requirement strings:

```kedi
> package: reports:
  source: src/reports
  python_dependencies:
    pydantic>=2
    httpx[http2]>=0.27; python_version >= "3.11"
```

`kedi install` and `kedi add` validate these requirements and install them into
the Python interpreter running Kedi. A venv-local Kedi command installs into
that venv; a command running on another Python installs into that Python.
The installer uses `sys.executable`, not an unrelated `python` or `pip` on PATH.
It uses that interpreter's pip, falling back to `uv pip --python` if pip is absent.
At least one of pip or uv must be available.

PEP 508 extras, version constraints, and environment markers are passed to the
Python installer together, without forcing an upgrade of satisfied requirements.
Imports and manifest inspection never trigger installation. Use the bundled
`require` module for runtime checks of optional, undeclared features.

If dependency installation fails, the Kedi installation fails without replacing
the previous package. Kedi does not roll back changes the Python installer may
already have made to the environment. Externally managed system Python policies
are respected; use a writable virtual environment when system installation is
not permitted.

## Kedi Dependencies

`kedi_dependencies` lists the Kedi packages a package needs: a package name,
optionally with a PEP 440 specifier.

```kedi
> package: release_tools:
  version: 1.0.0
  source: src/release_tools
  kedi_dependencies:
    pi>=0.1
    kedi_http
```

Names resolve through the registry, also when the package itself is installed
from a local path or a Git URL; an entry cannot name a path or a URL. The
package's own modules import a dependency like any installed package
(`> import: pi`). That import makes the dependency's adapters selectable in
the importing module (`> agent: pi`); modules that import the package do
not gain them. How installation and removal treat them is described in
[Package Commands](../tooling/package-commands.md#kedi-dependencies).

## Adapters

A package can expose agent integrations that importing modules select by
shortname, like the built-in ones. `adapters:` lists them:

```kedi
> package: pi:
  version: 0.1.0
  source: src/pi
  adapters:
    pi:
      kind: agent
      command: node bridge.mjs
```

```kedi
> import: pi
> agent: pi
> model: google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite
[summary] << Summarize README.md in one sentence.
```

Each entry has a `kind` and exactly one way to build it:

- `kind: agent` is selected with `> agent:` and must be an agent harness;
  `kind: adapter` is selected with `> adapter:` and must be an agent framework.
  Kedi checks the built adapter's kind and refuses one that differs.
- `command:` launches a [JSON-RPC bridge](../adapter-development/json-rpc-bridges.md).
  An argument naming a regular file of the package's `source` tree becomes that
  file's absolute path, so `node bridge.mjs` runs the installed file. A program
  that is not on `PATH` is reported before launch.
- `class:` names a Python adapter class as `module:Class`, which Kedi builds
  with `Class(model=...)`. The module comes from the interpreter running Kedi,
  usually through `python_dependencies`, and is imported only when a program
  selects the adapter.
- `environment: uv` runs a `command:` in a Python environment of the package's
  own, for a bridge whose harness pins what Kedi cannot share. See
  [Package Environments](../tooling/package-commands.md#package-environments).
  `environment_project:` takes that environment's uv project from a GitHub
  repository at an exact commit, for a harness that ships no wheel.

The shortname follows the package name rules and cannot be a built-in
adapter's. An import makes the package's adapters selectable in the importing
module only: modules that import that module do not gain them, and two imported
packages that declare one shortname fail at import. A procedure or profile
written where the package is imported keeps its adapter wherever it is called.

## Unknown and Duplicate Fields

Supported fields are `author`, `contact`, `license`, `version`, `source`,
`python`, `python_dependencies`, `kedi_dependencies`, and `adapters`, whose
entries take `kind`, `class`, `command`, `environment`, and `environment_project`. See the [Manifest Reference](../reference/package-manifest.md)
for their exact validation rules. Unknown fields, duplicate scalar fields, multiple
dependency blocks, multiple package directives, and a missing package directive
are errors.

Manifest validation happens before installation and again when an installed
package is resolved. A modified or incomplete installed manifest is treated as
registry corruption rather than trusted package state.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/local-package.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Distribution

# Build a Local Package

This deterministic package has no model or third-party Python dependency. It
separates a public module entry point from an implementation module.

## Files

```text
release_labels/
  package.kedi
  src/
    release_labels/
      main.kedi
      formatting.kedi
consumer.kedi
```

`release_labels/package.kedi`:

```kedi
> package: release_labels:
  version: 0.1.0
  source: src/release_labels
  python: python@3.11-3.14
```

`release_labels/src/release_labels/formatting.kedi`:

```kedi
@release_label(name: str, version: str) -> str:
  = <name> v<version>

> export:
  release_label
```

`release_labels/src/release_labels/main.kedi`:

```kedi
> import: formatting:
  release_label

> export:
  release_label
```

`consumer.kedi`:

```kedi
> import: release_labels:
  release_label

= <release_label(Kedi, 0.4.0)>
```

## Install and Run

From the directory containing `release_labels/` and `consumer.kedi`:

```sh
export KEDI_HOME="$PWD/.kedi-demo"
kedi install release_labels/package.kedi
kedi consumer.kedi
```

The consumer returns `Kedi v0.4.0`. The explicit absolute Kedi home keeps this
exercise separate from the normal user registry. Installation copies the
declared source; edits to the original need reinstallation. The receipt records
provenance but does not make the package trusted.

## What This Demonstrates

The internal `formatting` import resolves relative to `main.kedi`. Importers
receive exported bindings, not a namespace object. The package's Python version
range checks the installer interpreter; it does not download Python. See the
[manifest reference](../reference/package-manifest.md) for optional metadata
and dependency fields.

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/modules-and-packaging/installation-and-registries.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Distribution

# Installation and Registries

Kedi installs package source into a user-local registry. Installation validates
the manifest, Python compatibility, source containment, file kinds, and bounded
tree size before replacing an existing installed copy.

## Install a Local Package

From a package root:

```console
$ kedi install
Installed kedi_http ...
```

Or identify the manifest:

```console
$ kedi install path/to/package.kedi
```

The command validates and stages `package.kedi` and its declared source directory,
installs `python_dependencies` into the interpreter running Kedi, then commits
the staged package. The Kedi packages it lists in `kedi_dependencies` come from
the registry and install first, in the same transaction. Dependency errors leave the previous Kedi package intact.
Python environment changes are not part of the registry's atomic transaction.

Installing the same package name replaces the previous installation as one
validated transaction. Do not edit installed registry files manually; reinstall
from a source package.

## Add a Named Package

```console
$ kedi add textkit
$ kedi audit
```

Named add uses [the public Kedi registry](https://registry.kedi-lang.org).
It reads `v1/package/<name>.json`, rejects yanked or revoked packages, and
fetches the exact verified Git commit in that record rather than repository
HEAD. The manifest must match the registered package name and version.

`textkit` provides deterministic whitespace normalization, word counting, and
slug creation without a model or API key:

```kedi
> import: textkit

> show: <slugify(`"Release Notes"`)>
```

The output is `release-notes`. Named and Git installs automatically install
requirements listed in `python_dependencies` into the same interpreter running
the command. Dependency-free packages such as `textkit` do not run pip or uv.

### Development Registries

Set `KEDI_REGISTRY_URL` to use another HTTPS registry or a local HTTP server:

```console
$ KEDI_REGISTRY_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8767 kedi add textkit
$ KEDI_REGISTRY_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8767 kedi audit
```

Plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback addresses. Use the same registry
override for installation and subsequent audits.

For local registry-contract testing, set `KEDI_REGISTRY_MOCK_ROOT` to a directory
whose children are package source directories:

```console
$ export KEDI_REGISTRY_MOCK_ROOT=/absolute/path/to/mock-registry
$ kedi add kedi_http
```

The mock path is development infrastructure, not a production trust mechanism.

## Add an Explicit GitHub Package

```console
$ kedi add git+https://github.com/user/project.git
```

Kedi accepts credential-free `https` URLs hosted on `github.com`. It performs a
shallow, no-checkout clone with blob filtering, reads the root `package.kedi`,
and sparse-checks out only the declared source tree. The checked-out commit is
printed and recorded.

Arbitrary hosts, embedded credentials, unsafe source patterns, manifest
symlinks, and files escaping the checkout are rejected. A Git URL is an explicit
source install; it is separate from verified registry resolution and is reported
as `unverified` by `kedi audit`.

## Registry Location

The default home is:

```text
~/.kedi/
  registry/
    kedi_http/
      package.kedi
      .kedi-install.json
      src-or-copied-source...
```

Set `KEDI_HOME` to select the Kedi home used by package installation/resolution:

```console
$ export KEDI_HOME=/absolute/path/to/kedi-home
```

The override must be absolute. Relative values are rejected so changing the
working directory cannot silently switch registries.

## Installation Receipts

Each installed package has `.kedi-install.json` containing Kedi-owned provenance
such as source kind, source path, manifest digest, and, for Git, normalized URL
and commit. The receipt supports diagnosis and integrity checks; it is not a
signature or security audit.

Do not publish a source-owned `.kedi-install.json` and do not treat receipt
fields as package-controlled metadata.

## Audit Installed Packages

`kedi audit` reads receipts and checks the registry's `v1/audit.json` index once.
It does not execute imported packages, fetch repository HEAD, or update code.
Findings match the package name, repository, and exact verified commit; an
unchanged version string does not conceal a revoked commit.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | The installed commit remains active in the registry. |
| `superseded` | A historical commit, not withdrawn. |
| `yanked` / `revoked` | A withdrawn commit; review the registry's reason and replace it. |
| `unknown` | The verified commit is absent from the audit index. |
| `malformed` | The receipt or installed manifest fails validation. |
| `unverified` | A local or explicit Git source without verified registry provenance. |

`kedi audit` also prints a `DEPENDENCY` line for each installed package whose
Kedi dependency is missing or no longer satisfies it, and exits nonzero.

Exit code `0` means no actionable findings, `1` means a yanked, revoked,
unknown, or malformed installation, and `2` means the online audit could not
complete. `unverified` is not a security endorsement even though it does not
make the command fail. The audit checks manifest receipts and registry status,
not the contents of every installed source file.

## Source Safety and Limits

Installation accepts regular files and directories within the declared source
tree. It rejects path traversal, symlink escapes, special files, sparse-checkout
patterns, missing `main.kedi`, and trees exceeding configured count or size
bounds.

Installed-package resolution repeats boundary checks. It rejects a symlinked
package root or manifest, a directory name that disagrees with the manifest,
missing metadata, and source files outside the package.

These checks protect the registry layout and installation transaction. They do
not make package code safe to execute.

## Executable-Code Security

Importing a third-party Kedi package can execute its prelude, Python blocks, and
top-level statements with the Kedi process's host permissions. Review the exact
source and commit, install in an isolated Python environment, and restrict host
credentials and filesystem access as you would for any Python dependency.

A registry-verified commit pins identity and source provenance. It does not
sandbox behavior, prove correctness, or approve capabilities.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/reference/package-manifest.md
Section: Modules and Packages / Distribution

# Package Manifest Reference

## Complete Shape

```kedi
> package: reports:
  author: Kedi Team
  contact: maintainers@example.com
  version: 1.2.0
  source: src/reports
  python: python@3.11-3.14
  license: MIT
  python_dependencies:
    pydantic>=2
    httpx[http2]>=0.27
  kedi_dependencies:
    kedi_http>=1.0
```

The file must be named exactly `package.kedi`, contain exactly one package
directive, and contain no imports, exports, procedures, types, Python, values,
or executable statements. Comments are allowed.

## Fields

| Field | Required | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| package name | yes | `[a-z][a-z0-9_]*` |
| `source` | installable package: yes | literal relative directory containing `main.kedi` |
| `version` | no | valid PEP 440 version |
| `python` | no | fixed version or inclusive closed range |
| `python_dependencies` | no | one list of valid PEP 508 requirements |
| `kedi_dependencies` | no | one list of Kedi package names, each optionally with a PEP 440 specifier; no paths, URLs, extras or markers; not the package itself; each name once |
| `author` | no | metadata text |
| `contact` | no | metadata text |
| `license` | no | metadata text |
| `adapters` | no | one block of adapter entries (below) |

Unknown fields, duplicate scalar fields, a second dependency block, or a second
package directive fail validation.

## Adapters

```kedi
> package: pi:
  source: src/pi
  adapters:
    pi:
      kind: agent
      command: node bridge.mjs
    pi_local:
      kind: adapter
      class: kedi_pi:LocalAdapter
```

| Entry field | Required | Validation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| shortname | yes | `[a-z][a-z0-9_]*`, not a built-in adapter's (`pydantic`, `langchain`, `claude`, `codex`, `acp`, `a2a`, `rpc`, `dspy`) |
| `kind` | yes | `agent` (selected with `> agent:`, an agent harness) or `adapter` (selected with `> adapter:`, an agent framework) |
| `command` | one of `command` or `class` | a shell-style command line; arguments naming regular files of `source` become absolute paths |
| `class` | one of `command` or `class` | `module:Class`, a Python adapter class built with `Class(model=...)` |
| `environment` | no | `uv`, with `command` only: the command runs in an environment of the package's own, from the uv project (`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`) at the root of `source` |
| `environment_project` | no | with `environment: uv`: the uv project instead, as `git+https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY@<40-character commit>` (no tag or branch); every `environment: uv` adapter of a package names the same one, or none |

Unknown entry fields, duplicate shortnames or fields, and a second adapters
block fail validation. Nothing is imported or launched when a package is
installed or imported; Kedi builds the adapter when a program selects it, and
refuses it if its kind differs from the declared one.

## Python Requirement

Accepted forms:

```text
python@3.11
python@3.11-3.14
```

The range includes both endpoints and its upper bound cannot precede its lower
bound. Installation compares it with the interpreter running `kedi install`.
This field does not create or select a virtual environment.

## Source Tree

For `source: src/reports`, installation requires:

```text
package.kedi
src/
  reports/
    main.kedi
```

The package root import loads `main.kedi`; nested imports load sibling `.kedi`
files. Absolute paths, `..`, symlink escapes, sparse-checkout patterns, special
files, missing roots, and oversized source trees are rejected.

## Dependencies

`kedi install` and `kedi add` install `python_dependencies` into `sys.executable`,
the interpreter running Kedi. Pip is used when available in that interpreter;
otherwise `uv pip --python` targets the same interpreter. Requirement extras,
version constraints and environment markers retain their PEP 508 meaning.
Reading a manifest or importing a package does not install Python dependencies.

`kedi_dependencies` resolve through the registry, the same way as `kedi add <name>`. Kedi installs
them first, in one transaction with the package; see
[Package Commands](../tooling/package-commands.md#kedi-dependencies).

## Installation

```bash
kedi install
kedi install path/to/package.kedi
kedi add package_name
kedi add git+https://github.com/owner/repository.git
```

Installed content and `.kedi-install.json` receipts live below the Kedi home
registry. Named registry installs use an exact verified source commit. Identity
and integrity are not safety. Imported packages may execute Python with
the host process's authority.

---

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/agentic-engineering/index.md
Section: Agents and Orchestration

# Agents and Orchestration { #agentic-engineering }

Kedi treats model execution as scoped agent configuration rather than a global
string. A scope can select a framework or harness, model, reasoning effort,
instructions, settings, tools, MCP servers, skills, approvals, and child agents.

Choose the language construct by who controls the next step:

| Construct | Who selects the next step? | What it provides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procedure | The Kedi program | Explicit statements, arguments, return types, and captured configuration. |
| Profile | No execution by itself | Reusable configuration applied to later calls or used by a child agent. |
| Tool-using model call | The model, within the exposed tool surface | A request that may call tools before returning its result. |
| Subagent | The parent requests work; the child owns its conversation | An isolated task with its own profile and a bounded lifecycle. |
| Dynamic workflow | The parent writes orchestration code | Sandboxed composition of the permitted child agents. |

Start with a procedure when the sequence is known. Add a tool-using call where
the model needs to choose an action. Use a child agent when a task needs a
separate conversation and capability boundary, not merely a different prompt.

## Framework Adapters and Agent Harnesses

Framework adapters embed Kedi's prompt and tool contracts in an agent framework:

- `pydantic`
- `langchain`

Agent harnesses drive a complete external coding/agent runtime:

- `claude`
- `codex`
- `acp`

Select the first group with `> adapter:` and the second with `> agent:`. These
are mutually exclusive backend kinds, not interchangeable aliases.

## Active Agent State

Directives update immutable agent state for following calls in the lexical
scope:

```kedi
> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna
> effort: low
> instructions: Use tools only when they improve factual accuracy.
```

Top-level state is captured by following procedures. A procedure-body override
applies only to later calls in that invocation. When the scope exits, Kedi
restores the previous state.

## Profiles

Profiles name reusable state:

```kedi
> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > instructions: Review evidence before making a claim.

> use: reviewer
```

Profiles can be exported, imported, merged with later directives, and exposed
as direct child subagents.

## Capability Surfaces

- Procedures become typed tools through `> use:`.
- `> mcp:` attaches external MCP tools.
- `> skills:` exposes scoped registry, project, and user skill discovery.
- `> codemode: enabled` progressively discloses tools and executes hydrated calls in
  bounded code.
- `> approval:` controls risky tool calls.
- `> hooks:` observes, edits, or denies agent lifecycle boundaries.
- `> subagent:` adds bounded delegation tools to a profile.
- semantic stream events expose completed commentary and final messages to
  terminals, UIs, and orchestration code without changing adapter results.

Each surface is capability-checked against the selected backend. Unsupported
structured output is an execution error. Tools and MCP currently produce
forward-compatible editor warnings where an adapter may gain support later.

## Design Rule

Define the narrowest agent surface that can perform the task. Give profiles
specific instructions, only required tools, bounded child agents, and the least
permissive approval and sandbox settings. A broader model is not a substitute
for a clear contract.

# Instructions and Settings

Use `> instructions:` for scoped agent instructions. The old spelling
`> system:` is no longer accepted and produces a parse error. Replace the
name without changing the body; lexical scope and override rules stay the
same. Python's `system=` configuration parameter is unchanged.

Instructions define agent behavior; settings define adapter/model mechanics.
Both are lexical and apply to following calls.

Instructions express desired behavior; they are not permissions or enforced
invariants. Use typed captures for output validation, tool schemas for argument
contracts, and [approvals](approvals.md) for effectful operations. Asking a model
to "never write outside reports" does not replace a path check.

## Single-Line Instructions

```kedi
> instructions: Answer with evidence from available tools.
```

Use a single line for one stable rule. It is rendered when active state is
materialized.

## Multiline Instructions

```kedi
[audience] = maintainers

> instructions:
    Act as a release engineer for <audience>.
    Inspect evidence before reaching a conclusion.
    Report uncertainty explicitly.
```

Continuation lines are newline-joined. Multiline instruction bodies are read-only
templates: literal text, `<name>` substitutions, and inline Python
substitutions are allowed. Output fields and procedure calls are not.

A later `> instructions:` replaces the previous instruction value; it does not append
another paragraph. Compute one combined instruction explicitly when both parts
must survive. [Profile composition](profiles.md#merge-rules) uses the same rule.

For named reusable instruction contributions, use
[capabilities](capabilities.md). They append without changing profile override
semantics. A later explicit `> instructions:` clears those contributions as well,
including when the replacement text is identical. Runtime-owned instruction
sections are not removed.

```kedi
> instructions:
    Current audience: <audience>.
```

An instruction cannot declare `[output]` or call `<helper()>`; compute that
value before the directive and substitute the resulting variable. Use `<``>`
when the instruction itself must mention a literal triple-backtick fence.

## Runtime Instruction Sections

Kedi keeps scoped user instructions separate from its runtime rules. For an LLM
template with output captures, the runtime adds a `<TemplateInstructions>` section
to the request's instructions. The user message contains the field list and the
rendered template, without repeating the completion rules in its prefix or in
conversation history.

Profiles with tools, MCP, or enabled skills also receive a separate
`<ToolCallInstructions>` section. It covers evidence, explicit tool requirements,
permissions, and untrusted retrieved content. It does not prescribe a tool-use
strategy or require a lookup for every answer. The two sections are siblings,
not nested, and neither replaces the active `> instructions:` value.

When enabled, artifact and skill guidance use sibling `<ArtifactInstructions>`
and `<SkillInstructions>` sections. Built-in instruction XML tags, including
their internal headings, consistently use PascalCase. These headings do not
rename tool parameters, output fields, or serialized protocol data.

Raw invokes and claims do not receive template-completion rules. Jev and Laya
keep their decision-specific prompt semantics rather than sentence-completion
instructions. Runtime sections are assembled for the current call, not appended
to the stored user conversation on each turn.

These section names are internal prompt formatting, not Kedi syntax or security
boundaries. Typed validation and approval policies remain responsible for enforcing
contracts; provider caching still depends on the model and transport.

## Settings Blocks

```kedi
> settings:
    temperature: 0.2
    max_tokens: 1024
    parallel_tool_calls: false
```

Each setting has a value contract: booleans use lowercase `true`/`false`, numeric
fields accept numeric values, and option fields use their documented choices.
There is no generic `null`/`none` reset literal. Omitted settings retain their
default or inherited value; `tool_choice: none` is a documented string option,
not Python `None`. Containers and computed values require backticks.

Use backticks for explicit Python objects:

```kedi
> settings:
    stop_sequences: `["END", "DONE"]`
    extra_body: `{"mode": "json"}`
    parallel_tool_calls: `False`
```

Backticks are necessary for computed values and remove ambiguity about list,
dict, or object identity.

## Merge and Filtering

Settings merge by key. A later value replaces the same earlier key while
unmentioned keys remain:

```kedi
> settings:
    temperature: 0.2
    timeout: 30

@patient_call() -> str:
  > settings:
      timeout: 120
  >> The completed task's result is [answer: str].
  = <answer>
```

The inner call retains `temperature: 0.2` and uses `timeout: 120`.

Kedi validates setting names against its known public setting inventory, then
filters the merged mapping at the adapter boundary. Pydantic receives supported
`ModelSettings`; LangChain receives
its chat-model fields; harnesses receive their own process/runtime settings.

## Common Framework Settings

Common fields include `temperature`, `max_tokens`, `timeout`, `top_p`,
`parallel_tool_calls`, `tool_choice`, retry controls, stop sequences, and
provider extension bodies. Exact support still depends on the active adapter
and model provider.

Do not copy a provider-specific setting into every profile. Keep it in the
profile that owns that backend.

Pydantic AI and LangChain also support `request_retries` (a non-negative integer,
default `2`) for transient HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx model-request failures. It is a
Kedi policy, not a provider model parameter:

```kedi
> settings:
    request_retries: 1
```

Retries preserve history and completed tool results, remain inside the same
budget and deadline, and are independent of output/tool corrections. With
[fallback models](models-and-reasoning.md#ordered-fallback-models), each candidate
gets this bounded retry policy. `0` disables same-model retries, not explicit
fallback. Provider SDK retries are separate and must be disabled for strict
request budgets; Kedi does not mutate user SDK clients to do so.

## Harness Settings

ACP accepts `cwd`, `env`, and `timeout`. Codex accepts fields including `cwd`,
`sandbox`, `approval_policy`, `config`, `model_provider`, `service_tier`, and
`timeout`. Claude accepts fields including `cwd`, `env`, `tools`,
`allowed_tools`, `disallowed_tools`, `permission_mode`, `max_turns`, and
`max_budget_usd`.

```kedi
> agent: acp:
    command: npx @zed-industries/codex-acp
> settings:
    cwd: /workspace/project
    env: `{"LOG_LEVEL": "INFO"}`
    timeout: 120
```

`cwd` is passed to ACP, Codex, and Claude where supported. Relative child-agent
working directories are constrained by their parent safety boundary.

Claude appends `> instructions:` content to its Claude Code preset, preserving
built-in file behavior. Non-interactive Claude defaults to
`permission_mode: acceptEdits`; set tool and permission fields explicitly to
narrow it. Codex defaults to `workspace-write` unless settings narrow or replace
its sandbox.

## Settings Inventory

Kedi knows the keys below in `> settings:` (see `MODEL_SETTING_KEYS` in
`src/kedi/agent_profile/settings.py`). Any other name belongs to the adapter:
one that declares it takes it (a package adapter in `capabilities.settings`, a
JSON-RPC bridge in its handshake's `settings`), and any other adapter refuses
it before the first model request. Where no package adapter or bridge can be
selected (the module imports no package and has no `> agent: rpc:`), the
parser warns about such a name with `K-SETTING-KEY`. "Accepted by" names the
adapters whose boundary forwards the key; a key can still be filtered out
for a given provider or model. Value contracts come from the shared
directive-value registry (`src/kedi/directive_values.py`) where one exists.

| Key | Value contract | Accepted by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowed_tools` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Claude |
| `api_key` | Text value | LangChain |
| `approval_policy` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | Codex |
| `base_url` | Text value | LangChain |
| `callbacks` | Backtick Python object | LangChain |
| `config` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Codex |
| `configurable_fields` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | LangChain |
| `configurable_prefix` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | LangChain |
| `context_limit` | Model context window in tokens for Kedi's request ceiling | Kedi runtime |
| `cwd` | Path string | Claude, Codex, ACP |
| `decision_boolean_threshold` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `decision_tool_call_threshold` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `disable_streaming` | Disable streaming globally or during tool calls: `true`/`false` or `tool_calling` | LangChain |
| `disallowed_tools` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Claude |
| `env` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Claude, ACP |
| `extra_body` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `extra_headers` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `fallback_model` | Text value | Claude |
| `frequency_penalty` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `logit_bias` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `max_budget_usd` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | Claude |
| `max_retries` | Nonnegative integer | LangChain |
| `max_tokens` | Integer value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `max_turns` | Integer value | Claude |
| `media_limit` | Largest media value sent to the model (byte size, e.g. `100kb`) | Kedi runtime |
| `metadata` | Backtick Python list or mapping | LangChain |
| `model_kwargs` | Backtick Python list or mapping | LangChain |
| `model_provider` | Text value | Codex |
| `organization` | Text value | LangChain |
| `parallel_tool_calls` | Boolean: `true`/`false` | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `permission_mode` | Text value | Claude |
| `personality` | Text value | Codex |
| `presence_penalty` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `rate_limiter` | Backtick Python object | LangChain |
| `reasoning` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | LangChain |
| `reasoning_effort` | Text value | LangChain |
| `request_retries` | Additional attempts for transient model request errors | Kedi runtime |
| `response_cache` | Boolean: `true`/`false` | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `response_cache_ttl` | Positive integer | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `sandbox` | Filesystem sandbox policy: `read-only`, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access` | Codex |
| `seed` | Integer value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `service_tier` | Provider service tier: `auto`, `default`, `flex`, `priority` | Pydantic AI, Codex |
| `stop` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | LangChain |
| `stop_sequences` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `stream_usage` | Boolean: `true`/`false` | LangChain |
| `streaming` | Boolean: `true`/`false` | LangChain |
| `summary` | Text value | Codex |
| `tags` | Backtick Python list or mapping | LangChain |
| `temperature` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `thinking` | Thinking budget: `true`/`false` or `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` | Pydantic AI |
| `timeout` | No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter | Pydantic AI, LangChain, Codex, ACP |
| `tool_choice` | Tool selection policy: `none`, `auto`, `required` | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `tool_reason` | Activation: `enabled`/`disabled`, or a backtick expression returning `bool` | Kedi runtime |
| `tools` | Backtick Python list or mapping | Claude |
| `top_p` | Numeric value | Pydantic AI, LangChain |
| `voice` | Voice name for speech output (`[x: Audio] <<`) | Kedi runtime |

## Unknown and Inapplicable Settings

Unknown setting names are parser/LSP errors. A known union-level key can still
be irrelevant to a selected backend and is filtered rather than passed
blindly. Adapter docs list the exact mapping.

Prefer a minimal settings block. Every additional provider knob is part of the
profile's operational contract and should have a tested reason.

Conversation history and compaction are intentionally not model settings. Use
`> history: enabled` for stateful calls or the expanded history policy described
in [Caching and Conversation History](../runtime/caching.md).

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/agentic-engineering/profiles.md
Section: Agents and Orchestration / Profiles and Configuration

# Profiles

Profiles can also select a lexical native history processor through
`> history:` with `enabled: true` and ``processor: `callback` ``. This overrides
the adapter constructor default only for the scoped invocation. See
[History Processing](../runtime/history.md#native-configuration) for callback
types, explicit disable, safe group retention, and lineage.

Profiles are named, reusable agent configuration. A profile describes how a
model call should run: its backend, instructions, tools, permissions, and optional
children. Defining or applying a profile does not start a model call, create a
conversation, or run its tools.

A procedure describes executable steps; a profile supplies configuration to
those steps. A child profile describes a separate agent invocation that a parent
may request. These are different roles even when they share the same tools.

[Capabilities](capabilities.md) are the separate additive surface for reusable
tool and instruction bundles. A profile may use them with `> use:` without
changing its own override semantics.

## Define a Profile

```kedi
> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Reviews one change against repository evidence.
    ###
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > effort: medium
    > instructions: Cite the evidence used for every finding.
    > settings:
        timeout: 120
```

A profile body contains directives, not an executable procedure body:

| Concern | Members | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend | `adapter`, `agent`, `model`, `fallback`, `effort` | Select execution backend, primary model, ordered alternatives, and reasoning behavior. |
| Instructions | `instructions`, `settings` | Supply instructions and supported runtime/model settings. |
| Tools | `use`, `mcp`, `skills` | Expose procedures, external tools, and skill discovery. |
| Permissions and lifecycle | `approval`, `hooks` | Mediate sensitive calls and lifecycle boundaries. |
| Context | `history`, `artifacts` | Configure conversation retention and artifact handling. |
| Tool execution | `codemode` | Enable the code-based tool interface. |
| Child agents | `subagent`, `max_agents`, `workflow`, `output` | Define delegation, its budget, orchestration mode, and a default child result type. |

Choose either `adapter` or `agent` on one selected profile path, not both. Profiles are
top-level declarations. Tools referenced by the profile must exist; declaring
their names does not implement them.

## Conditional Configuration

Group related settings under a deterministic condition instead of repeating the
same expression in each field:

```kedi
[detailed_review: bool] = `True`

> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > if: `detailed_review`:
        > model: openai:gpt-6.1-sol
        > effort: high
        > instructions: Explain each finding using repository evidence.
    > else:
        > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
        > effort: medium
        > instructions: Return only actionable findings supported by evidence.

> use: reviewer
```

The guard must return an exact Python `bool`. It runs once when the profile is
applied, in the same environment as its computed fields. Unselected expressions
and uses do not run. The selected members contribute to the profile in source
order; later members can override them. Without `> else:`, a false condition adds
nothing. Guards can nest and selected branches may contain `> use:`.

This is configuration selection, not an executable body: templates, calls,
returns, and model-evaluated claims are not allowed as members or guards. The
closing colon after the Python expression is required. Both branches are checked
for valid members. A selected path cannot contain both `agent` and `adapter`, or
multiple `output` or `workflow` members in one profile. A dynamic workflow must
have a child after its selected configuration has merged.

When applied before a procedure definition, the selected configuration is captured
there; changing the guard's inputs later does not rewrite the captured profile.
Editor analysis does not execute guards. Runtime validates selections it cannot
prove statically.

## Profile Documentation

When a `###` block is the first profile member, it becomes the profile
docstring. The LSP shows it in hover and subagent tool descriptions. A later
block remains an ordinary comment.

Document what task the profile owns, what evidence it should return, and any
important limitation. Child-agent descriptions depend on this text.

## Apply a Profile

Single-line `> use:` applies a profile when no procedure with that name exists:

```kedi
> use: reviewer

>> A review of the current change is [review: str].
= <review>
```

If a procedure and profile share a name, the procedure wins and is registered
as a tool. Avoid such collisions.

## Merge Rules

Applying a profile merges it into the state already active at that location.
It is not a reset to an empty configuration:

| Member | Composition rule |
| --- | --- |
| Backend, model, effort, instructions, approval, output type, maximum starts, workflow mode | A specified value replaces the earlier value. Instructions are replaced, not concatenated. |
| Fallback models | Replace the entire ordered list; omission inherits, and ``> fallback: `[]` `` clears it. A model override alone does not clear it. |
| Settings | Merge by key; later values replace the same key. Nested dictionaries are not recursively merged. |
| Tools and children | Merge by name. Later bindings win, and reintroduced names move to the end of the ordered list. |
| MCP servers | Append in declaration/application order. |
| Hooks | Compose per event; a supplied empty handler list clears that event's local handlers. Inherited enforcement is a separate boundary. |
| Skills, CodeMode, history/compaction | Supplied configuration replaces the corresponding earlier configuration. |
| Artifacts | Overlay the explicitly supplied policy fields. |
| Omitted members | Keep their earlier values. |

These are ordinary profile merge rules. Capability-owned resources are stricter:
conflicting concrete bindings or approval policies fail instead of transferring
ownership to a later same-named tool. An explicit instruction replacement also
clears preceding capability guidance, without removing its tools or policies.

An empty tools list is not a request to revoke tools inherited through profile
composition. For a separate restricted agent, define a child with its own tool
surface and use [delegation](subagents.md). See [Hooks](hooks.md) for inherited
handlers that child code cannot disable.

Direct directives after profile application can override profile members:

```kedi
> use: reviewer
> effort: high
```

The result retains the reviewer's configuration and changes effort to `high`.
The selected provider must support that effort value.

Profile application and direct directives follow source order. A direct directive
does not have unconditional priority: a profile applied after it can replace it.
Procedures capture the configuration at their definition site; see
[Scoping and Capabilities](scoping-and-capabilities.md).

`> fallback:` may be the only model-selection member in a profile. It uses the
effective inherited primary and needs no adjacent `> model:`. The primary must
resolve before invocation; a backup is never promoted implicitly. Procedures,
conditional members, and subagent profiles retain normal lexical capture rules;
local list replacement leaves the caller unchanged. Fallback is supported by
Pydantic AI and LangChain, not harness adapters or capability bundles. See
[Ordered Fallback Models](models-and-reasoning.md#ordered-fallback-models).

## Default Child Result Type

```kedi
~Finding(path: str, explanation: str)

> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Reviews supplied evidence and returns actionable findings.
    ###
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > instructions: Base findings only on the evidence supplied in the task.
    > output: list[Finding]
```

When a parent delegates to `reviewer` without supplying `final_schema`, this
output type supplies the child's result schema. The returned envelope contains
`run_id`, `subagent`, `task_summary`, and the validated `final_result`.
An explicit `final_schema` on the child call takes precedence over `> output:`.
Without either schema, the child returns its text in `task_summary` and has no
structured result.

This is a child-result contract, not a way to change the types of unrelated
template captures. A template's `[finding: Finding]` still declares its own
output type. The profile type must be representable as JSON Schema; declaring
two `output` members is an error.

## Export and Import Profiles

Profiles are module values and can be explicitly exported:

```kedi
> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna

> export:
  reviewer
```

Imported profiles retain private tool and child-profile bindings needed by
their contract without flattening those dependencies into the importer's
procedure namespace. This lets a package expose a profile facade while keeping
helpers private.

## Forward References and Validation

A profile can name a child profile declared later. Kedi resolves the complete
profile graph and rejects unknown children and cycles.

On one selected profile path, framework and harness selection remain mutually exclusive.
Invalid backend kinds, unknown members, duplicate output/workflow declarations, invalid settings,
nonpositive `max_agents`, missing tools, and unsupported required capabilities
produce diagnostics or compile-time errors.

## Child Profiles

```kedi
> profile: coordinator:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > subagent: researcher
    > max_agents: 3
    > workflow: dynamic

> profile: researcher:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > instructions: Investigate one self-contained question.
```

Only directly listed children can be delegated to. `max_agents` bounds the
descendant work started by one parent invocation. Workflow mode defaults to
`delegate`; `dynamic` exposes one sandboxed Python orchestration tool. See
[Subagents](subagents.md) for lifecycle and safety rules.

## Choosing Profile Boundaries

Create a profile when a task needs a stable combination of behavior and
capabilities. Do not create one merely to alias a model string. Profiles should
be narrow enough that their tools, approvals, and child relationships can be
reviewed as a coherent security boundary.

Source: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/agentic-engineering/capabilities.md
Section: Agents and Orchestration / Profiles and Configuration

# Capabilities

!!! note "Unreleased"
    This page describes the next Kedi release. Eager composition is supported by
    Pydantic AI and LangChain; deferred loading is supported by Pydantic AI only.

A **profile** selects agent configuration. A **capability** contributes reusable
instructions, tools, and tool-local policies without replacing the host model or
base instructions. Both are applied with `> use:`. Neither starts a model call.

Use a [subagent](subagents.md) when the contribution needs a separate model,
conversation, or execution loop.

## Compose Instructions

```kedi
> capability: evidence:
    ###
    Separate observed facts from assumptions when assessing readiness.
    ###
    > instructions: Use the supplied evidence and identify unfinished checks.

> capability: concise:
    > instructions: Keep the explanation to one sentence.

> profile: release_reviewer:
    > instructions: Assess whether the release can proceed.
    > use: evidence
    > use: concise

> use: release_reviewer
>> Unit tests passed, but staging verification is still running.
The release readiness is [readiness: Literal["ready", "pending"]],
because [reason: str].
= `{"readiness": readiness, "reason": reason}`
```

The request receives the profile's release-assessment instruction followed by
the evidence and concise contributions. The docstring describes the capability
in the editor and, when deferred, in its discovery catalog. The example needs
a configured model, just like any other template program.

Use `> use:` inside a profile to compose capabilities. There is no separate
`> capabilities:` directive. A capability may itself use another capability or
a tool, but cannot use a profile to import host-wide configuration indirectly.

## Reset, Then Reuse

Using the definitions above:

```kedi
> use: release_reviewer
> instructions: Report only the observed deployment state.
>> Staging verification is still running, so its status is [status: str].

> use: concise
>> The current status of <status> means [explanation: str].
```

The first request has only the new user instruction. The second also has the
concise contribution. An explicit instruction assignment clears prior user
guidance even when the new base text equals the old text.

Resetting instructions does **not** remove tools, capability approval, hooks,
history, or runtime instructions such as the template-filling contract. Reusing
a capability restores its guidance once; repeated use does not duplicate it.
Deduplication uses capability identity, not matching instruction text.

Profiles still override. A profile with explicit instructions replaces the
current user instruction composition; a model-only profile does not. Profile
members follow source order: instructions after capability use clear earlier
guidance; capability use after instructions appends to the new base.

## Contribute Tools

This exportable review module is a small building block for a harness. It reads
a caller-supplied source file and returns a typed finding, not a complete coding
agent or a sandbox.

````kedi
```
from pathlib import Path
```

@read_source(path: str) -> str:
    ###
    Read a UTF-8 source file for inspection.
    ###
    = ```
    source = Path(path)
    return source.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    ```

> capability: source_reader:
    > instructions: Read the named file before describing its implementation.
    > approval: allow
    > use: read_source

> instructions: Review code without changing files.
> use: source_reader

@review_file(path: str) -> str:
    >> The most significant concrete issue in <path> is [finding: str].
    = <finding>

> export:
    source_reader
    review_file
````

The local allow policy belongs only to `read_source`; it does not allow unrelated
host tools. An explicit policy on the exposed tool takes precedence, then the
capability policy, then the calling agent's default. Independent mandatory
enforcement still applies. A procedure's internal `> approval:` governs its
internal agent calls, not whether the outer caller may invoke that procedure.

Tools retain their concrete definition-site bindings when imported. Exporting
the capability does not export its private procedures separately. Incompatible
ownership or policy for the same tool name is an error, not last-writer-wins.

The example reads paths allowed by the process. Instruction text and capability
names do not impose filesystem restrictions; enforce those in the tool or its
execution boundary when needed.

## Local Procedure Instructions

Procedures capture the configuration visible at their definition site. A local
`> instructions:` replaces that invocation's inherited user guidance, while
captured tools remain available. A later local capability use appends there.
Returning, failing, or cancelling the procedure does not alter its caller.

This is not a fresh conversation and does not erase history. A procedure declared
before a later base instruction does not acquire that later instruction, even
when it had no base instruction at its definition site. The same rule applies
across notebook and IDLE cells.

A procedure with no model binding still falls back to the invoking agent's
model, as before. That inference fallback does not import the caller's later
instructions or tools; an explicitly captured model continues to win.

## Deferred Loading

Using the source tool defined above:

```kedi
> capability: source_reader_on_demand:
    ###
    Read source files when implementation evidence is required.
    ###
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Read the requested source file before answering.
    > use: read_source

> use: source_reader_on_demand
```

Without `defer`, use is eager: tools and guidance are available for the next
request without a discovery call. With `defer: true`, the native Pydantic AI
loader exposes a catalog entry first. Tools cannot execute until activation,
even if the model guesses their names. Repeated loads are idempotent.
This means registrations and activation are not duplicated; the native loader
may return a retry response for an already-active capability.

`defer` also accepts an inline Python expression returning an actual boolean.
Kedi evaluates it once per use context, not on every model retry. Strings and
numbers are not accepted as truthy substitutes.

The initial adapter contract is Pydantic AI eager/deferred and LangChain eager
only. Unsupported adapter combinations fail before inference. Nested deferred
capabilities and deferred subagent targets are supported on Pydantic AI.

Deferred instructions can remain in historical load results after a reset.
Reset suppresses their automatic reinjection; it does not make the model forget
history. Explicit reuse restores guidance only after native activation. Native
MCP setup/catalog discovery may occur before loading, so deferral is not a
promise of lazy connections or zero resource cost.

### Nested Capabilities

Using `read_source` from the earlier example:

```kedi
> capability: implementation_evidence:
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Read the named source before making implementation claims.
    > use: read_source

> capability: code_review:
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Distinguish observed defects from suggestions.
    > use: implementation_evidence

> use: code_review
```

Initially only `code_review` is discoverable. After the native loader confirms
its activation, `implementation_evidence` becomes discoverable. Loading that
second capability makes `read_source` callable. Loading the parent does not
automatically load its deferred child; parent and child load calls in one model
response do not skip that boundary. Eager child contributions become available
with their deferred parent.

A shared child has one stable registration even when multiple parents include
it. Any activated parent makes it discoverable. Explicit direct use also makes
that child discoverable independently of its parents. These are contribution
and loading relationships, not a sequence of tasks or separate agents.

### Deferred Subagent Targets

```kedi
> profile: evidence_reviewer:
    > instructions: Review supplied evidence and identify unsupported conclusions.

> capability: specialist_review:
    > defer: true
    > subagent: evidence_reviewer

> use: specialist_review
```

The child profile is captured when the capability is used. Its target becomes
available to the shared delegation or dynamic-workflow tools only after loading
`specialist_review`. Guessing the target before activation does not start a child
or invoke its capability-owned hooks. If the host already has other subagents,
their shared controls remain available, with only those active targets exposed.

Background work, waiting, continuation, and messaging keep the captured binding
and ownership checks. The subagent's own model and instructions remain those of
its profile. CodeMode catalogs and schema results obey the same target visibility
and activation rules as native calls.

Reset suppresses guidance throughout the nested contribution graph while retaining
registrations. Reuse restores guidance once, still gated on native activation.
If two deferred parents share a child and only one parent is reused after a
reset, the child's guidance returns only after that parent and the child are
loaded. Loading the other parent alone does not restore the child's guidance;
the order of the parent declarations does not change this behavior.
Each run owns its activation; sharing an adapter or descriptor does not share
loaded state. Revealing a nested catalog changes its instruction prefix, so this
path does not guarantee prefix-cache preservation.

## Conditional Contributions

Use deterministic guards to choose an instruction/tool bundle or its loading
policy. The capability still contributes resources, not agent-wide overrides:

```kedi
[needs_citations: bool] = `True`

> capability: evidence_policy:
    > if: `needs_citations`:
        > instructions: Support factual conclusions with supplied sources.
    > else:
        > instructions: Clearly distinguish suggestions from observed facts.

> use: evidence_policy
```

The Python expression must return an exact `bool` and is evaluated once per
application. Only the selected branch's computed values and uses run. Nested
guards and optional `> else:` follow the same rules as
[conditional profile configuration](profiles.md#conditional-configuration).
Selected instructions remain additive to the host's base instructions. Selected
approval and hooks remain limited to this capability's owned tools. A selected
`> defer: true` makes the resulting capability load on demand; it does not defer
the guard itself. Unselected tools are not registered.

All branches must respect the configuration boundary below, including branches
whose guard is false. A condition is not a way to add model selection or other
caller-owned settings to a capability.

## Configuration Boundary

| Capability member | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `instructions` | Owned instruction contribution; local replacements affect only its bundle |
| `use`, `mcp`, `subagent` | Contribute tools, MCP sources, or child-profile bindings |
| `approval` | Override the default for owned concrete tools only |
| `hooks` | Owned tool lifecycle events, retaining mandatory enforcement |
| `requires` | Declare adapter requirements, not permissions |
| `defer` | Choose immediate contribution or native on-demand loading |

Host `model`, `fallback`, `effort`, `settings`, `agent`, `adapter`, `output`,
`history`, budgets, skills discovery, CodeMode policy, and artifacts are rejected at the
capability root. `user_prompt_submit` hooks and `tool_reason` remain agent-wide.

Use the calling agent's artifact `exclude_tools` for exact-name exceptions.
Exclusion does not disable approval, reason, output limits, or tracing. See
[Artifact Policy](../runtime/artifact-policy.md) and [Hooks](hooks.md).

## Inspect Behavior

Telemetry records application/reuse, instruction replacement, request snapshots,
native load attempts and activation, tool ownership and approval source, and
artifact admission decisions. CodeMode retains the actual inner tool span.
Capability IDs are stable hashes; source locations require source-path capture.
Instruction content follows the existing content capture policy.

Deferred loading can change request prefixes. Cache reuse depends on the
provider and transport; it is not guaranteed. Capability loading does not require
schema search or CodeMode, and is not automatically more efficient than a small
eager tool set.

See [Python Capability Definitions](../python-api/capabilities.md) for the same
composition contract through `kedi.Capability`, and the
[adapter capability matrix](../reference/capability-matrix.md) for support checks.
